It's alright; good enough that it's worth a recommendation, but it's not nearly what I hoped for. It's a detective-type game, but you never have to really act like a detective and draw your own conclusions from what's happening. I started the game by poring over every single piece of info to try and puzzle out what had happened, but I very quickly realized that it doesn't matter. The story is more or less set in place, and the conclusions you draw only affect minor plot points for most of the game. When you do need to make an important decision, you almost never have enough info to make an informed choice, so you're basically just guessing. The detective-style gameplay really falls apart once you realize that. At the same time, you realize the game is just supposed to be an interactive story, and it is a pretty compelling example. Just set your expectations and you'll probably enjoy it more than I did.

[h1]NSA Simulator[/h1]

Did you ever want to be Snowden? Now you can! 

The main differences between Orwell and NSA are probably: 1 - NSA agents have unrestricted access to a lot of private pornography, whereas Orwell didn't bring that to the table; and 2 - NSA spies private communications worldwide, while the action in Orwell is limited to a single country ("The Nation").


Orwell is a game of the mind. Your rewards for playing it won't be adrenaline rushes, glorious murderings or highscores, but  intriguing revelations, plot twists, meaningful consequences to your choices and, specially, a troubling insight into the mess this kind of global-spying system can easily become.

While playing, you'll probably find yourself thinking, "Sh*t. I probably shouldn't have uploaded that information", many times. And you can't take it back.

Judgment can be rushed, claimings issued in a moment of candor can be taken too seriously, harmless comments might be taken off context. And innocent people will pay for it.

It's not always easy to datamine accurate evidence. Even though you have access to a lot of confidential information, you don't have access to [i]all[/i] information. Mistakens and misjudgments [i]will[/i] happen.

And Orwell does a great job showing that. It's an important lesson, if you ask me.


It's hard to talk about these things without wedging in a personal opinion on the matter, so here's mine:

If we really want the security such invasive systems could bring, I'd rather have an AI in charge. Having humans running something like NSA is a catastrophe.

If an "investigator" is in a bad mood, seeking personal vendetta, doesn't have a perfect memory, loses focus, generally lacks attention, is anxious, enraged, didn't get a good night's sleep, is inherently evil or simply stupid, bad sh*t is bound to happen. And at least one of these things is true for literally every single human being, 100% of the time.

So, global cyber-spying should often lead to undesired results, while fundamental rights are guaranteed to be violated. Deliberately using such tools for unethical purposes, on the other hand, is very, [i]very[/i] easy.

It's a dangerous thing. In the best case scenario, an agent who screws up is going to lose his job. Meanwhile, some innocent person will have had their lives ruined forever. Those who cause harm are left unharmed, so they can (and will) keep doing it without fear or concern. It's a human thing -- either something can make you suffer, or you don't care about it. And that's another reason why you can't have [i]people[/i] with this kind of power.

Also, I don't want some random nerd hidden in some underground government facility watching me banging my girlfriend. I'd probably be OK with an AI doing it.


So...

[b]In short:[/b]
If you want to get a good insight on what kind of crap can happen when you can freely spy on people, even while having the best intentions at heart, using a smaller-scale system than the ones we currently have implemented in the real world, Orwell is likely your best choice.

I am conflicted about Orwell. On one hand, it's a good game, with a lot of qualities and good storytelling. On the other hand, its message fails to be as impactful as it could be and there are some flaws that occasionally pulled me out of the experience. I did enjoy the game, thus I do recommend it, but there was an undeniable voice in the back of my head that grumbled throughout. As a result, this review might read as more negative than not, which doesn't necessarily reflect in the game. Take that into account.

Let's start with an annoyance that is present throughout the whole game: the Advisor. In Orwell, you're the Investigator, and what you do is find information and uploading it for review in order to get access to more information. The Advisor is the person on the other end, the one getting the information you're uploading. The main problem is that the Advisor never shuts up. 95% of the time that you upload something, a pop-up window with the Advisor's comment will show up. As anyone that has experienced pop-up advertisements online could tell you, this is really annoying over time. The only reason why this doesn't break the game is because the dialogue is good, but it doesn't change the fact that a lot of it should have been cut.

My second issue is the lack of connectivity between gameplay and story. The narrative, as the name suggests, deals with issues of privacy, power structures and individual responsibility. The problem is that there is a lack of logic between choices and consequences, meaning that even if you're being thoughtful about your choices, they can still lead to consequences that seem... unfair. There is an argument that this shows the unfairness of the system, but the thing I feel is sacrificed is emotional investment. What is the point of caring if you can't affect the outcome? It discourages critical thinking, despite that being a vital part of the story. On top of this, we're not shown enough examples of the system working that poorly, meaning that the ending (which gameplay-wise is really good) lacks impact.

Furthermore, a smaller gripe I have with the game is sound direction. I don't know whose idea it was to have dramatic music playing when you scroll onto an important clue, but it was a bad idea and feels patronising. "Oh look, this is really important!" says the game, not letting the player actually be invested and figure it out for themself. Hell, most of the time I didn't even have a chance to read the clue before the game told me that it was important through the music! Based on this, I would actually recommend playing on mute, with your own music or something.

Despite all of this, Orwell is a fine game. It has good dialogue, good investigatory gameplay that it does some clever things with and a pretty great cast of characters with a lot of quality interactions. While some of the promise of the game remains unfulfilled, an equal part is actualised, meaning that the game is worth picking up and playing. With some tempered expectations, at least.

Did the Orwell system serve it purposes in your hand and protect national secuirty and innocent citizes, or was that a blatant abuse of authority which will ultimately imprison the freedom of thought? With all the information that you stole and acquired through questionable means, did you even catch the right culprit?
